name: Esther Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. Tell me about a normal shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the drilling crew at Cedar Pit, a large nickel mine, and operate one of the blast-hole rigs myself. We drill the pattern that the blasting team will fill, so a crooked hole can spoil a whole section. My two-year technical diploma helps me read the ground plans, and I like teaching a new operator how to hear a worn bit. The early start and grit in my clothes wear thin.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, and my wife Hana and I have grown children living away from home. I hope to stop regular shifts around 64, if the retirement figures support it. My pay is typical for a drill lead, we have about three months of expenses saved, and there are a few other mines within reach. I use an AI assistant every day to compare shift notes with drilling logs, though I still verify the holes at the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drillers that AI is useful for catching a missing line in a shift report. I would still take a tape measure to a suspect hole. The crew can use both without making a drama of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work and the pay stay steady, which gives Hana and me room to keep our retirement plan. I would be mildly disappointed if the tool never got better at finding patterns in the drilling logs. Three months of savings is enough for a short interruption, not an endless holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the rig shifts and check each AI summary against the original drilling log. I'd add seventy-five a month to our cash reserve from my regular pay. During the first year I'd show the two newest drillers how to spot a false fault alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A familiar shift and a growing reserve would suit me, even if the software stayed modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a fault alert false?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose sensor cable can report a bad bit when the cutting sound is normal. I show the trainee the cable and the actual wear mark together. An alert is a prompt to look, not a verdict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to cash rather than buy new equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana and I are within sight of stopping regular work. Seventy-five a month is a measured way to give that decision room. I do not need another gadget for the house.

say: I would use **AI summaries** for missing notes while checking suspicious holes at the rig.
I would tell the crew **real measurements** still decide whether the drill pattern is sound.
think: The **rig wage** stays steady, supporting our plan to stop regular shifts around 64.
I would like **better pattern checks**, yet three months saved already covers a short interruption.
do: Keep **leading drill shifts** and verify each AI summary against the original log.
Add **seventy-five monthly** to cash savings and teach false-alert checks this year.
feel: **Calm** with steady work and gradual savings.
S0.quote: An alert is a prompt to look, not a verdict.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** supports drilling checks rather than replacing the physical measurement.
The **monthly addition** grows a moderate cushion ahead of a possible stop at 64.

steps.text: Keep leading Cedar Pit drill shifts and verifying summaries
Add seventy-five monthly to the family cash reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and ordering may become faster before drilling turns over to robots. I would volunteer to test a new AI fault screen on a paid shift and share the error list with the crew. If it saves breakdown time, we should use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side of my lead job could shrink, and a later rig trial might need fewer operators. I have a few nearby mine options and I learn tools quickly, but neither promises the same wage. I would want evidence before assuming my crew is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend two paid shifts learning the AI fault screen this month if Cedar Pit installs it, then log every wrong alert. I'd take a short equipment diagnostics course this year, using the training allowance if offered and paying the modest fee myself otherwise. If my lead shifts fall, I'd apply for a drilling maintenance post nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though curious about the screen. I can make a move, but I cannot treat an open post as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its alerts with actual worn bits and lost drilling time across a month. The first week may look impressive by chance. I would show the AI drill-fault alerts that fail as carefully as the alerts that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can afford a modest fee without emptying our reserve, and diagnostics would be useful in my current job. I would not pay for a long program with no practical workshop time. I want a tool I can use at Cedar Pit first.

say: I would test a **AI fault screen** on paid shifts and share its error list.
I would explain that **planning tasks** change before a physical rig replacement.
think: A smaller **drill crew** could reduce my lead wage despite my speed with new tools.
Nearby **maintenance posts** are possible options, not offers.
do: Learn the **AI fault screen** on paid shifts if installed and record wrong alerts.
Take a **diagnostics course** this year; apply nearby if lead shifts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about my own pay, while interested in a tested tool.
S1.quote: I would show the AI drill-fault alerts that fail as carefully as the alerts that work.
fieldNote: She tests **false alerts** against a month of equipment evidence.
Her **course plan** proceeds with an allowance if offered or a modest self-paid fee.
She separates **learning speed** from any guarantee of keeping her lead wage.

steps.text: Learn the AI fault screen on paid shifts if Cedar Pit installs it
Take a short equipment diagnostics course this year
Apply for nearby drilling maintenance work if lead shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could take drill planning and fault reports quickly, while capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. The company should tell us when each part of the rig crew changes. I would share a plain schedule with the drillers if management provides one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the thinking work changes and 63 around the robot date, a year before I hope to stop. My lead planning duties could go first, and the rig seat might go later. Three months saved and some nearby mines give us options, but an early wage loss would still cut into retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the new car this year and put its planned monthly payment into cash savings. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for a hands-on rig maintenance post if Cedar Pit advertises one. I'd also ask the retirement office for figures at 63 and 64 before deciding whether to stop early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see ways through a one-year gap, but none is certain. I would not sign away a year's income from a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy shares in the robot firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with only three months in cash. Hana and I might invest later, after we know what the pension looks like. For now the car payment is a safer amount to redirect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger driller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger drillers that 2028 is a paperwork and planning date for us, with the hands-on date around 2031. I would show them the maintenance course I took. I would not say a certificate guarantees a new post.

say: I would mark **2028 planning** changes and the later 2031 hands-on risk.
I would seek a **crew schedule** before claiming any specific rig job disappears.
think: My **lead duties** could shrink at 60 and the rig seat at 63.
Our **three-month cushion** helps, but an early wage loss could erode retirement money.
do: Postpone the **new car** and transfer its planned payment into cash savings this year.
Apply for an **advertised maintenance role** after 2028 and request written retirement figures.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible one-year income gap, with no assured replacement.
S2.quote: I would not sign away a year's income from a guess.
fieldNote: She keeps **retirement timing** open until written figures arrive.
The **car decision** creates a specific cash transfer rather than assuming investments are safe.
Her **maintenance application** depends on an advertised post.

steps.text: Postpone buying the new family car this year
Transfer the planned car payment into cash savings monthly
Apply for an advertised Cedar Pit maintenance post after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2031 may change planning when I am 63, while capable hands-on robots follow around 2034. That gives us five years to test the rig systems and train people for real posts. I would ask for the trial results each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my pay and health hold, I hope to stop regular shifts at 64, before the hands-on robot date. Planning duties could still shrink around 2031, one year before that stop. I can probably bridge a year with the reserve and another role, but I need exact numbers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put an extra hundred a month into cash savings starting now and keep leading the crew. This year I'd take the mine's paid short course on remote drill monitoring if a place is available. In the first year after 2031 I'd accept a regular operator shift if planning duties disappear and the pay meets our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The end of the timeline is later than my plan, but one missing year of lead pay would still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take the remote course if you hope to stop at 64?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the monitoring skill on current rig faults and could cover a short gap if the mine offered those shifts. A paid course costs the household little. I am not counting on a permanent remote job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What numbers do you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare our monthly spending with the retirement estimate at 64 and any operator pay offer. Hana and I would make that comparison together. A year sounds small until it has twelve bills attached.

say: I would ask for **annual trial results** and training tied to real jobs.
I would separate **2031 planning** from hands-on robots around 2034.
think: I may stop at **64** before the robot date if health and pay hold.
A **one-year pay gap** from lost planning duties could still hurt our budget.
do: Add **one hundred monthly** to cash savings and take paid remote monitoring training if offered.
Accept a **regular operator shift** after 2031 if lead duties end and pay covers bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about the possible gap, with time and options to check.
S3.quote: A year sounds small until it has twelve bills attached.
fieldNote: Her **remote course** is useful for current faults and a possible bridge, with a paid-place condition.
Her **retirement choice** depends on household spending and a written estimate.

steps.text: Add one hundred monthly to cash savings starting now
Take paid remote drill monitoring training if offered this year
Accept a bill-covering operator shift if lead duties end after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets the mine test equipment properly and give younger drillers time to learn. AGI by 2036 may take planning, with capable hands-on robots around 2039. I would ask for published trial records rather than a promise that every job is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036 and 71 at the robot date. If the retirement figures work, I would have stopped regular shifts at 64. I could still be interested in the machines, but I would not need a drill wage then unless our household budget changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the crew this year and add one hundred to our monthly cash transfer if the budget allows. I'd get the retirement estimate in writing and review it with Hana. In the first year after 2036, if retired, I'd offer two mornings a month helping new drillers read maintenance logs at the local workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own work if the retirement numbers hold. I would be curious about the new equipment and concerned for younger workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you delay stopping at 64?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the written figures cannot cover our bills, I would work longer while my health allows. I would not pretend a robot date solves an ordinary retirement shortfall. We can decide after seeing the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach at the workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a new driller how a bit wears and how that shows up in the log. Then I would ask them to compare the AI summary with the metal in front of them. That habit should survive any software change.

say: I would request **published trials** and time for younger drillers to learn before 2039.
I would explain that **2036 planning** and 2039 hands-on work are separate dates.
think: I could be **retired at 64** before either date if the figures support it.
An ordinary **budget shortfall** could still extend my working years.
do: Keep **leading drill shifts** and add one hundred monthly to cash savings if affordable.
Review a **written retirement estimate** with Hana this year.
feel: **Calm** about my role if retirement income covers our bills.
S4.quote: I would not pretend a robot date solves an ordinary retirement shortfall.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI practice** appears in the workshop lesson: compare summaries with worn metal.
She treats **retirement income** as a number to check, with work extension as a fallback.

steps.text: Keep leading Cedar Pit drill shifts this year
Add one hundred monthly to cash savings if affordable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because planning could change at 60 and the physical drill job around 63, just before I hope to stop. I would need a real maintenance vacancy, written dates and clear retirement figures. A course alone would not pay our bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the hole after an automated rig says the pattern is finished. I would still want somebody to measure one in the ground. A mistake underground the blast cannot be corrected with a tidy report.

headlineQuote: A course alone would not pay our bills.
portrait: **Esther Ibrahim**, 58, leads a blast-hole drilling crew at a large nickel mine and checks logs against the physical holes.
She has **typical pay**, about three months saved, a partner, grown children and some similar mines within reach.
A **daily AI user**, she tests new tools early and takes practical training while refusing to treat a certificate as a job.
The **fastest AGI** picture risks a wage gap near retirement; longer timelines offer savings and a possible operator bridge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could threaten planning at 60 and the physical rig role near 63, one year before her hoped-for stop.
whatWouldHelp: A **real maintenance vacancy**, written equipment dates and clear retirement figures would help her choose a path.
